full_judgment:
10. An admission of a person is admissible in evidence as against him, though it can he explained away by the maker thereof or the person against whom it is sought lo be proved. According to me, the same principle applies to an admission in a signed pleading, or in affidavit, or in any swam deposition given by a party in a prior litigation, though it is capable of rebuttal. The assertion of a right, whether in a pleadings or other statements, is relevant under section 13 of the Evidence Act and is, therefore, legally admissible in evidence; Phipson on Evidence, Ninth Edition, at page 455 stated that "pleadings are admissible, in subsequent proceedings, to prove their own existence, the institution of the suit, and the facts in issue between the parties. But being regarded in other respects rather as the suggestions of counsel than the declarations of the parties, they are not receivable to prove the truth of the facts stated, even as admissions, unless verified by oath, or signed or otherwise specifically adopted by those against whom they are tendered". In Satyadeo Prasad V. Smt. Chanderjoti, AIR 1966 Pat 110, it was argued that an admission in a signed pleading filed in an earlier suit by the predecessor of the defendant could be used against his successor, inasmuch as, an admission contained in a plaint or written statement or an affidavit or any sworn deposition given by a party in a prior litigation will be regarded as an admission in a subsequent action, though it is capable, of rebuttal. Similar views have been taken in S.T. Chendikamba V. K.I. Biswanathamayya,  AIR 1939 Mad 446. It was pointed out that what a party himself admits to be true may reasonably be presumed to he so, but the party making the admission may give evidence to rebut this presumption and unless and until that is satisfactorily done the fact admitted must be taken to be established. 

 22. The question is not the competency of P.W.1 to depose of behalf of the plaintiff. The question is reliability of a particular witness to prove a fact in issue. The first duty of a Court being to ascertain facts about which the parties are at issue. Section 5 of the Evidence Act may be described as the corner stone of the structure of Part-I of the Evidence Act which specifies the facts that may be given in evidence. Since a fact in issue is the necessary ingredient of the litigated right or liability, it may be given in evidence as a matter of course. It is a fundamental rule that unless there is some presumption as to existence of a fact, its existence must be proved to the satisfaction of the Court. Therefore, the party who wishes the Court to believe in the existence of a fact, must prove it. Whether a, witness should or should not be believed is one of peculiar difficulty owing to perjury that pervades the atmosphere of Courts in the country. Questions as to what a Court to do on this particular point can never be solved by any artificial rules of evidence or procedure as argued by Mr. Mahmudul Islam, and the best guide of a Court on such questions is its common sense and experience of human nature. Facts which are neither admitted nor are subject to judicial notice must he proved. The Evidence Act attaches more importance to the quantity than to the quality of evidence by providing that no number of the witnesses is in any case required for the proof of any fact. Proof of a fact would depend upon the character of the witness and his competency to speak to that fact.
